summary: This unit teaches you to lead a welding and fabrication team through a job. You will learn to plan the work, estimate person-hours, draw a bar chart, share out and delegate tasks, give clear instructions, run toolbox talks and meetings, and keep track of progress and quality. You will also learn to solve problems, manage changes, motivate and coach people, induct new members, settle conflict fairly, lead on safety, and keep the diary, handovers and reports.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A **team leader** is the link between the supervisor and the people doing the work. You make sure the job is done **safely, on time, to the right quality and within the resources** given, and you often still work on the tools yourself.

Good welders do not automatically make good team leaders. Leading means planning before acting, talking and listening, being fair, dealing with problems early, and keeping records. This unit teaches those skills, using the jobs a fabrication team does every day.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who leads, or will lead, a small team in a workshop or on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Read the job details, list the tasks, estimate the time, put them in order, draw a bar chart, check resources and set hold points.
Give tasks by skill, qualification, workload and development; delegate with clear authority and check points.
Give instructions people understand, run toolbox talks and short meetings, and record agreed actions.
Set daily targets, measure output and quality, and act early when the team falls behind.
Find root causes with facts, and handle client changes in writing, with a new plan.
Motivate, give feedback, coach, induct new members, settle conflict and treat everyone fairly.
Make sure controls and permits are in place, let anyone stop unsafe work, watch for fatigue, report incidents.
Keep a job diary, report progress and delays, hand over properly, and write the end-of-job report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, sharing out work, communication, meetings, monitoring, problem solving, leadership, motivation, conflict, safety and reporting, with some sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and sums such as person-hours, percentages and overtime pay) and longer answers explaining what you would do as team leader.
**Practical tasks**: as a team, plan and make a small fabricated item, with each member leading one stage; and a team meeting role play to solve problems, agree actions and write a progress report.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms such as SMART, KPI (key performance indicator), SDS (safety data sheet), storming, delegation, debrief, OSH (occupational safety and health), autocratic and non-verbal communication.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Your duty to
What it involves
rows: Plan it; get the resources; keep it on time, safe and to quality; solve problems; report progress
Clear instructions, fair treatment, training and support, recognition, a safe place to work
Follow its policies and procedures, keep records, look after equipment and materials, control cost

blocks.p: The Centre's (or company's) **policies** set the rules on safety, discipline, grievances, leave and absence, harassment and equal treatment, drugs and alcohol, and the use of phones. Know where to find them (the staff handbook or the policy file), apply them the same way to everyone, and ask the supervisor or human resources when you are unsure. Jamaica's employment law sets the minimum terms for hours, overtime and leave, and the policies put them into practice.

head: Style
How it works
Best for
If overused
rows: The leader decides and gives clear orders, with little discussion
Emergencies such as a fire or injury; jobs with only one safe method; a new, inexperienced team
People feel ignored, motivation falls, good ideas are lost
The leader asks for ideas and involves the team, then decides and takes responsibility
Planning a job, improving a method, solving a quality problem, especially with an experienced team
The leader leaves decisions to the team
A highly skilled, motivated team on familiar work
Without checks, work drifts and people are confused

blocks.p: A good leader changes style to fit the situation and the people: directive when speed and safety demand it, participative when there is time and the team's experience can help.
Most teams go through four stages (Tuckman's model). Knowing the stage helps you choose what to do.

head: Stage
What you see
What the leader does
rows: People are polite, unsure and look to the leader
Set clear goals, roles and rules; introduce people; give direction
People test each other; disagreements and conflict are common
Listen, deal with conflict early and fairly, restate roles and rules
The team agrees ways of working; trust grows
Involve the team more, build good habits, start to delegate
The team works well and solves its own problems
Delegate, support, recognise good work, develop people

blocks.p: When the job ends and the team breaks up (sometimes called adjourning), thank people and hold a debrief. A team can slip back a stage when people join or leave, or the job changes.

flow: Read the job details: drawings, specification, order, delivery date, budget
List every task
Estimate the time for each task in person-hours
Put the tasks in order and find the dependencies
Draw a bar (Gantt) chart; mark hold points and key dates
Check resources: people and skills, materials, consumables, equipment, space, permits
Order long-lead items first
Share out the tasks
Brief the team

blocks.p: A **person-hour** (often called a man-hour) is one person working for one hour. Estimate each task in person-hours, then:

blocks.note: Days needed = total person-hours ÷ (number of people × hours each works per day)
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Example:** a job needs 150 person-hours, and the team has 4 people working 7.5 hours a day. The team works 4 × 7.5 = 30 person-hours a day, so the job takes 150 ÷ 30 = 5 days.

ul: Allow for setting up, breaks, inspection, weather on site and things going wrong: add a margin (contingency).
Adding people does not always speed a job up: there may be only one plasma cutter, or one welder qualified for a coded weld.

blocks.p: A **dependency** is a link where one task cannot start until another finishes: painting waits for weld inspection; welding waits for fit-up. Tasks that do not depend on each other can run **in parallel**, at the same time.

A **bar chart (Gantt chart)** lists the tasks down the side and the days across the top, with a bar for when each task starts and how long it lasts. Arrows show dependencies and a diamond marks a key date such as delivery. It shows everyone who is doing what each day, and you can shade the bars as work is done to show progress.

The longest chain of linked tasks is the **critical path**: here A–B–C–D–E–F, 12½ days. It sets the finish date, so **any delay on it delays the finish**. Task G is not on it and has spare time (float): it can slip a little without delaying the job.

ul: A **hold point** is a stage where work stops until it has been inspected, for example the first item checked before the rest are made, or welds inspected before painting.

Set goals that are **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Work hard this week" is not SMART; "weld and inspect all 12 frames by Thursday at 3 p.m., with no more than one repair" is.

head: Resource
Check
rows: Skills, qualifications (for example a welder qualified for that procedure and position), leave, absence
Ordered in time; delivery checked against the order
Electrodes, wire, gas, discs, paint: enough, and the right kind
Hot work permits, site access, lifting arrangements

blocks.p: Check materials and equipment against the plan **before** the job starts. A missing item found halfway through stops the whole team.

ul: Share tasks by **skills, qualifications, experience and current workload**.

Work that needs a qualification goes **only** to someone who holds it, current, for that procedure and position. If only one person is qualified, plan the job around them, and think about training others.
Give newer members tasks they can learn from, with support and checks, not the hardest job "to test them".
Only people trained on a machine (a magnetic drill, a forklift, a plasma cutter) use it.
Share unpopular jobs and overtime fairly, in turn, through an open system, and explain your decisions. Never share work by favouritism.

blocks.p: **Delegation** is passing a task, **and the authority to do it**, to a team member. You still keep the **responsibility** for the result.

flow: Choose the task and the right person
Explain the result needed, the deadline, the standard and the limits of their authority
Give them the information and resources
Agree check points
Let them get on with it, without taking it back or redoing it behind their back
Review the result, give feedback and recognise good work

head: Why delegate
What not to delegate
rows: Frees the leader to plan and lead
Tasks the person is not trained or qualified for

blocks.note: Delegating is not dumping. Give the person a clear brief and the support they need, and check at the agreed points. Never checking is as bad as checking every five minutes.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Plan what you will say before you say it.
Choose the place: go somewhere quiet, or have nearby machines switched off, for anything important.
Use short sentences and plain words. Explain trade terms.
**Show as well as tell**: point at the drawing, hold up the part, demonstrate the method.
Give one step at a time, then ask the person to **repeat back** the key points, so you know they understood.
Invite questions, and follow up later.
For important or complicated work, give it in writing as well.
When a drawing or method changes, **issue the new document and brief everyone**. A message passed from person to person gets changed or lost.
Use sketches, marked-up drawings and demonstrations for people who find reading hard, and help them privately, without embarrassing them.

Many people talk in Jamaican Patois at work and read English less easily. That is fine; make sure written instructions are explained in plain words and understood. Never make fun of how anyone speaks.
Respect differences in age, faith and background. Listen as well as speak.

blocks.p: **Non-verbal communication** is the message sent by body language, facial expression, gestures and tone of voice, without words. Watch for signs that someone is unsure or unhappy: a frown, silence, avoiding your eyes, or nodding but not acting. Your own body language matters too: folded arms or looking at your phone while someone speaks tells them you are not listening. In noisy areas, agree simple **hand signals** for stop, wait, come here, lift and lower.

ul: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety briefing, about 10–15 minutes, at the work area at the start of the work.
Pick one or two hazards of **today's** tasks, for example zinc fumes when cutting galvanised pipe, a heavy lift, or hot work near a doorway, and the controls.
Make it two-way: ask questions to check understanding, and invite concerns and near misses.
Everyone signs the attendance sheet. Brief anyone who arrives late before they start work. Keep the sheet with the job records.

head: Meeting
What it is for
rows: Same time each day, 10–15 minutes: progress against the plan, problems, today's plan, safety
One problem: the facts, the causes and the actions
After a job: what went well, what to do better next time

ul: Have an **agenda**; start and finish on time; keep to the topic.
Make sure everyone is heard, not just the loudest.
Write down every decision and **action: who does what, by when**, so nobody is in doubt, then follow it up.

blocks.p: Texts and group chats are useful, but do not assume a message has been read or understood. Confirm anything important face to face, keep work chats professional, and keep confidential matters out of group chats.

ul: Set **daily targets** from the plan: parts cut, joints welded, frames painted.
Check progress at set times: walk the job, ask the team, count finished work and mark it on the progress chart.
Check **quality** as well as quantity. Work that must be redone is not progress: count it only when it has passed inspection.
Compare actual progress with the plan every day, so a problem is caught while it is small.

head: KPI
How to work it out
Example
rows: 72 welds by 3 people in 6 hours = 72 ÷ 18 = 4 welds per person-hour
Days ahead of or behind the plan

flow: Spot it early by comparing progress with the plan
Find the cause: missing material, a breakdown, absence, rework, or a task that was under-estimated
Agree a fix with the team: move a person, get the machine repaired, change the order of work, ask for approved overtime or extra help
Never cut safety checks or inspection to catch up
Tell the supervisor as soon as you know the finish date is at risk
Record what happened, so future plans are better

blocks.note: Long hours make people tired, and tired people make mistakes and have accidents. Keep overtime limited, approved and shared, keep breaks, and in a hot workshop make sure people drink water and rest.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Define the problem with facts
Gather the data
List possible causes (brainstorm, fishbone diagram)
Find the root cause (5 whys)
Choose and try a fix
Check that it worked
Make it standard and share it

head: Why?
Answer
rows: The base plates were not cut on time.
The plasma cutter was out of action for a day.
Why was it out of action?
There is no minimum stock level for them.

blocks.p: The **5 whys** reach the root cause: no minimum stock level. Setting one, with someone responsible for re-ordering, stops the problem coming back. Blaming the operator would not.

ul: When a client asks for a change, get it **confirmed in writing** by someone with the authority to approve it.
Check what it does to the time, cost, materials and safety, and tell the supervisor.
Re-plan, issue the revised drawing, withdraw the old one, and brief the team.
Record the request and the approval in the job diary.
**Recognise good work**: thank people specifically for what they did, and share successes with the whole team.
Share the goals and the results, so people know what they are working towards.
Involve the team in decisions that affect them.
Treat everyone fairly, and give people the right tools, training and clear expectations.
Threats, secret plans and sudden changes with no warning destroy motivation.

head: Good feedback is
Poor feedback is
rows: Specific: "The last three fillets have undercut on the top toe."
About the work, not the person
Private, when it is about a problem
Balanced: what is good, and what to change
Two-way: asks the person what they think is causing it
Ends with an agreed plan and a follow-up

flow: Explain what good looks like, and why
Show the method yourself, or have a skilled welder show it
Let them try it on scrap
Watch and give specific feedback
Let them practise more
Check the result, and record the coaching

ul: Plan the induction before they arrive, and welcome them.
Introduce the team and key people: the supervisor, the first aider, the store clerk.
Show them the emergency exits, assembly point, extinguishers, first-aid kit and welfare areas.
Explain the safety rules, PPE, hot work rules and how to report hazards and incidents.
Explain the job, their role and who to ask for help.
**Check their skills and qualifications** before giving them tasks, and pair them with an experienced member (a buddy) for the first days.
Explain hours, breaks and the main policies. Have them sign the induction checklist.
Meet them again after the first week to see how they are settling in.

blocks.p: Conflict at work usually comes from shared equipment, workload, unclear roles, misunderstandings, personality clashes or pressure from outside work. Left alone, it spreads and hurts the work.

flow: Act early
Talk to each person privately and listen without taking sides
Find the real cause
If both agree, bring them together somewhere quiet; keep to facts and the work
Help them agree a solution
Write down what was agreed
Check later that it is working
Report bullying, harassment, threats or safety risks, or a conflict you cannot settle, to the supervisor, and follow the procedure

head: Way of handling conflict
What happens
When it fits
rows: Both sides work out a solution that meets both their needs
Important, lasting problems, when there is time
Each side gives up part of what it wanted
A fair split is needed quickly, such as sharing one machine
Emergencies and safety rules, where there is no room for debate
When it matters much more to the other person
The issue is left alone, for now
Trivial matters, or to let tempers cool before talking

ul: Treat everyone with respect, whatever their sex, age, religion, background, where they come from or any disability.
Stop remarks and "jokes" that put people down as soon as you hear them, and remind the team of the rules on respect.
When someone complains of unfair treatment, listen, check the facts, follow the procedure and keep it confidential.

blocks.note: A Jamaican workshop brings together people from town and country, of different churches, ages and backgrounds. Judge the work, not the person, and the team will trust you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Everyone** is responsible for safety. The team leader sets the example, and makes sure the controls are in place before work starts.

ul: Identify the hazards of each task and check that the risk assessment and its controls are in place: screens, extraction, guards, extinguishers.
Make sure each person has the training and PPE they need, and uses it.
Make sure equipment is checked before use.
Get the right **permits**: hot work, confined spaces, lifting, work at height.
Keep the **safety data sheets (SDS)** for paints, thinners, gases and other chemicals, and brief the team on them.
Give a toolbox talk on the day's hazards.
Make sure anyone can **stop unsafe work** and report a hazard without fear of blame.
Make sure the team knows the first-aid and emergency arrangements.
Watch for fatigue and heat stress.
Report problems you cannot fix to the supervisor.

blocks.note: Jamaica's workplace safety law sets duties for employers and for workers, and the Ministry of Labour and Social Security inspects workplaces. The Centre's safety policy and procedures put those duties into practice: follow them, and make sure your team does.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Make the area safe
Give first aid, or call the first aider and emergency help
Report it to the supervisor
Record it in the accident book or on an incident report, even a minor burn or cut
Look into the cause
Agree actions to stop it happening again
Share the lessons with the team

blocks.p: Near misses are reported in the same way. They are free warnings: the next time, someone may be hurt.
Keep a daily job diary or log. It is the record of what happened and why, and it settles arguments later.

ul: The date and the weather (on site)
Who was working
Work done against the plan
Materials received
Problems and the decisions made
Instructions received: from whom, when and what
Visitors, incidents and near misses
Photos where they help
Report progress against the plan, problems, actions taken and any help needed: short and factual.
Report a **delay as soon as you know about it**, not when the client complains. Early warning gives the supervisor time to act.

blocks.p: When you hand the job to another leader, at the end of a shift or before leave, give a written handover and walk the job with them:

ul: Progress, and what is unfinished
Hazards
Open permits and isolations
Equipment problems
Materials expected
The next steps

head: Part of the report
Why it is useful
rows: So it can be filed and found
Results against the plan: output, time, materials, cost
So future jobs are planned and priced better
So quality problems can be tracked
Safety: incidents, injuries, near misses, actions
To give credit and plan training
So the next job goes better

blocks.p: Keep the report clear, accurate and honest, with photos or charts where they help, and date and sign it.
A **debrief** is a short meeting after the job to review what went well and what could be better. Everyone is heard, the lessons are written down, and they are used in the next plan.

head: Sum
Example
rows: 7.5 hours a day for 5 days = 37.5 hours
Time-and-a-half on J$1 200 an hour = 1.5 × 1 200 = J$1 800 an hour; double time = J$2 400

blocks.p: Overtime is paid at the rate in the contract and the law; time-and-a-half is common.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and talk it through with your instructor.

ul: I can describe the team leader's duties to the job, the team and the business.
I can choose a leadership style to suit the situation, and say which stage a team has reached.
I can list a job's tasks, estimate them in person-hours and work out how many days the job will take.
I can draw a bar chart with dependencies, find the critical path and set hold points.
I can write SMART goals and check resources before a job starts.
I can share out tasks fairly by skill, qualification and workload.
I can delegate a task with clear authority and check points.
I can give clear instructions and check they were understood.
I can read non-verbal signals and communicate with people of different backgrounds and reading levels.
I can run a toolbox talk and a short meeting with an action list.
I can monitor progress and quality with KPIs, and act when the team falls behind.
I can use the 5 whys to find a root cause, and handle a client change properly.
I can motivate the team, give useful feedback and coach a skill.
I can induct a new team member.
I can settle a conflict fairly and stop disrespectful behaviour.
I can lead on safety, including permits, stop-work, fatigue and incident reporting.
I can keep a job diary, hand over a job and write an end-of-job report.
I can work out hours, overtime pay and percentages of target.

terms: The leader decides alone and gives orders without asking the team
A chart showing when each task starts and how long it lasts
The longest chain of linked tasks; it sets the finish date
A short meeting after a job to review what went well and what to improve
Passing a task, and the authority to do it, to a team member
A link where one task cannot start until another finishes
Spare time a task has before it delays the finish
Passing a job to another leader, with progress, hazards and next steps
A stage where work waits for inspection before it goes on
Introducing a new member to the people, rules, safety and job
The daily record of work, problems, instructions and decisions on a job
Key performance indicator: a measure of how well the team is doing
Messages sent by body language, expression and gestures, without words
The leader involves the team in decisions, then decides
One person working for one hour
The cause which, if removed, stops a problem coming back
Safety data sheet: the supplier's information on a product's hazards and safe use
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound
The team stage where members test each other and conflict is common
A short safety briefing at the start of work
Asking "why?" again and again to reach the root cause

c1.title: Fence panels for a school in Port Maria
c1.text: Garfield leads a team of five making 24 steel fence panels for a primary school in Port Maria, St Mary: himself; Leroy, the most experienced welder; Ackeem, who is careful at marking out; Shawna; and Tevin, who joined two weeks ago. The panels are estimated at 180 person-hours of work, Garfield adds 20 person-hours for setting up and inspection, and the team works 8 hours a day. Painting cannot start until the welds are inspected, and welding is on the longest chain of linked tasks.

c2.title: Cattle-pen gates in Santa Cruz
c2.text: A team of four in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, must make 30 cattle-pen gates in five days, six a day. By the end of Wednesday, 17 gates have been made: 14 passed inspection first time, and 3 were rejected for undersized welds and are waiting for repair. On Tuesday the guillotine was out of action for four hours, and on Wednesday one welder was off sick. The supervisor, Mr Henry, suggests working 14-hour days for the rest of the week.

c3.title: A boat-repair yard in Lucea
c3.text: At a boat-repair yard in Lucea, Hanover, two welders, Romaine and Dexter, both need the yard's only TIG set for aluminium work, and they have started arguing in front of the others. Mrs Gordon, the team leader, notices that apart from this, the team now plans its own work, shares tools without fuss and sorts out small problems without her. This week, three of Romaine's hull seams showed porosity at the start of the weld.

c4.title: A new starter in Morant Bay
c4.text: Latoya, a newly qualified welder, joins Desmond's fabrication team in Morant Bay, St Thomas, on Monday morning. The shop is loud with grinders most of the day. Mr Brown, who has many years of experience, finds reading difficult. On Tuesday the team starts cutting galvanised pipe for a school's handrails, and a revised method statement for the job has just been issued.

c5.title: A market roof in Chapelton
c5.text: Andrea leads the team building a steel roof for a market shed in Chapelton, Clarendon, for the municipal corporation. Halfway through, the council's project officer telephones to ask for the roof overhang to be 300 mm longer, and written approval arrives two days later. In the second week, three members each work 8 hours of overtime, paid at time-and-a-half on a normal rate of J$1 200 an hour.

questions.q: With his allowance added, how many working days should Garfield plan for?
o: 4.5 days
4 days
5 days
6 days
questions.why: The total is 180 + 20 = 200 person-hours, and the team works 5 × 8 = 40 person-hours a day, so 200 ÷ 40 = 5 days. Leaving out the allowance gives 4.5 days, a plan with no room for set-up or inspection.

questions.q: How should Garfield use Tevin on this job?
o: Give him the welding, so that he learns fastest
Keep him sweeping until the job is finished
Let him choose whichever task he likes best
Pair him with Leroy on tasks he can learn
questions.why: New members learn best on suitable tasks with an experienced partner and checks on their work. Giving them the most demanding work, or no real work, helps neither the person nor the job.

questions.q: Welding falls one day behind. What happens to the finish date if nothing else changes?
o: Nothing, as painting can start early
It slips by about half a day
It slips by a day
It is not affected by welding
questions.why: Welding is on the critical path, the longest chain of linked tasks, so a delay there delays the finish. Painting cannot start early because it must wait for the weld inspection.

questions.q: Which of these is a SMART target for the team's first week?
o: Work as hard as possible and keep the school happy
Do better welding than the last team that did fencing
Make good progress on the panels by the end of the week
Weld and inspect 12 panels by Friday at 3 p.m.
questions.why: A SMART target is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Twelve inspected panels by a set time can be checked; the others cannot.

questions.q: What percentage of Wednesday's target has the team reached?
o: About 78%
About 94%
About 47%
About 82%
questions.why: The target by Wednesday was 3 × 6 = 18 gates. Only the 14 that passed count as done, so 14 ÷ 18 × 100 ≈ 78%. Counting the rejected gates would wrongly give 94%.

questions.q: How should the three rejected gates be counted on the progress chart?
o: As finished, since they have been made
As finished, but marked with a small note
As half done until the repairs are made
As not done until repaired and passed
questions.why: Work that must be redone is not progress. Counting rejected work as finished hides the real position from the leader and the supervisor.

questions.q: Which plan is the best way to recover the lost time?
o: Work 14-hour days to the end of the week, as suggested
Skip the inspection on the rest of the gates
Re-plan, with two evenings of approved overtime
Let the newest member weld gates unchecked
questions.why: Limited, approved overtime with a revised plan recovers time without cutting safety or quality. Very long days cause fatigue and mistakes, and skipping inspection only moves the problem to the farm.

questions.q: What is the team's first-time pass rate so far?
o: About 82%
About 78%
About 18%
About 47%
questions.why: First-time pass rate = gates passed first time ÷ gates inspected × 100 = 14 ÷ 17 × 100 ≈ 82%. It measures quality, while output against target measures progress.

questions.q: Apart from the TIG set dispute, which stage of team development has Mrs Gordon's team reached?
o: Storming
Norming
Performing
Adjourning
questions.why: A team that plans its own work, shares resources easily and solves its own problems is performing. The leader can delegate more, while settling the one dispute quickly.

questions.q: Romaine and Dexter agree that one will have the TIG set in the mornings and the other in the afternoons, and neither gets all he wanted. Which way of handling conflict is this?
o: Avoiding
Compromising
Accommodating
Competing
questions.why: In a compromise each side gives up part of what it wanted to reach a fair split. It suits sharing one machine when a quick, fair answer is needed.

questions.q: Which feedback to Romaine about the porosity is most likely to help?
o: "Your work has been poor lately and you need to pull your socks up."
"Everybody else's welds are passing this week, so why are yours failing?"
"Three seams had porosity at the start; let's check your gas cover."
"Don't worry about the porosity; I will grind those seams out myself later."
questions.why: Useful feedback is specific, about the work, and leads to a shared plan. Vague criticism, comparisons with others, and quietly fixing the work all leave the cause in place.

questions.q: How should Desmond make sure Mr Brown understands the revised method statement?
o: Leave a copy on his bench to read at home
Talk him through it with the drawing and the part
Ask Latoya to read it out to him in front of the team
Assume he knows it, since he has many years of experience
questions.why: Showing and explaining the changes, privately and with the drawing in hand, gets the message across without embarrassing him. Experience does not tell anyone what has changed in a new revision.

questions.q: During Monday's briefing, Latoya nods but frowns and looks at the floor. What should Desmond do?
o: Take the nod as a sign that she has understood
Repeat the whole briefing more loudly for everyone
Tell her to look at him when he is talking to her
Check with her privately afterwards
questions.why: Her body language suggests doubt or worry even though she nodded. A private, friendly check gives her a chance to ask without feeling exposed in front of a new team.

questions.q: Which topic best suits Tuesday morning's toolbox talk?
o: The bonus scheme for finishing early
Zinc fumes and how to control them
How to fill in the timesheet correctly
The plan for next month's jobs
questions.why: A toolbox talk covers the hazards of the day's work. Cutting galvanised pipe gives off zinc fume, so the talk covers the fume, the extraction and the respirators to use.

questions.q: Which arrangement is best for Latoya's first week?
o: Give her the hardest weld on the job to see what she can do
Let her watch for the whole week before she does anything
Check her skills, then pair her with an experienced member
Let her choose the tasks she likes, so that she settles in
questions.why: Checking her skills shows which tasks suit her, and a buddy helps her learn the shop's ways safely. Testing her on the hardest weld, or leaving her idle, does neither.

questions.q: Written approval for the longer overhang has arrived. What should Andrea do before the team starts on it?
o: Re-plan, issue the revised drawing and brief the team
Start at once, as the team already knows about the call
Wait for the council to send someone to oversee the work
Ask the team to vote on whether to make the change
questions.why: A change affects materials, time and sometimes safety, so the plan is updated, the old drawing replaced by the revised one, and everyone briefed before work starts.

questions.q: What should Andrea write in the job diary about the project officer's telephone call?
o: Nothing, since a call is not a written instruction
Only that the client wants to change something
Her own opinion of the change and of the officer
Who called, when, what was asked and agreed
questions.why: A clear diary entry records who asked for what, and when, which matters if time or cost is questioned later. Personal opinions do not belong in the job diary.

questions.q: How much overtime pay do the three members earn in total?
questions.why: Time-and-a-half is 1.5 × J$1 200 = J$1 800 an hour. Three people × 8 hours × J$1 800 = J$43 200.

questions.q: A team leader hands Kayon the weekly ordering of consumables, with the authority to place orders. What stays with the leader?
o: Responsibility for the result
The authority to place the orders
Placing every order personally
None of it: all of it passes to Kayon
questions.why: Delegation passes the task and the authority to do it, but the leader stays responsible for the outcome. That is why check points are agreed and the results reviewed.

questions.q: An experienced team has two weeks to find ways to cut porosity in its aluminium welds. Which leadership style suits best?
o: Directive: decide alone and announce it
Participative: seek ideas, then decide
Delegative: leave it all to the team
No style: let whoever is free decide
questions.why: With time available and an experienced team who know the work, involving them uses their knowledge and builds commitment. The leader still makes and owns the final decision.
